1qrGwX9kQoQ: Earlier this year, a bunch of us on the team who make SciShow got together at a retreat in New Orleans. This is a real video, don’t worry. Stick with me. And some of us wanted to take in the local culture at Mahogany Jazz Hall. We were enthusiastically welcomed by a hostess named Lexi, who hooked us up with some delicious absinthe cocktails and told us a bunch of interesting stories about the science of absinthe. The next morning… after a couple glasses of water… we decided to dig further into the topic, and it was just as fascinating as she promised. Indeed, we uncovered a historical mystery. For decades, absinthe was outlawed across Europe and North America due to its supposed hallucinogenic properties. But thanks to some recent studies, the true source of its psychedelic reputation is beginning to emerge. Absinthe is a spirit flavored with a distinct combination of herbs, including anise and wormwood. Wormwood has medicinal properties – it’s useful against, well, worms. These properties were known to the ancient Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians. But it’s much more recently that someone had the idea of putting it in cocktails. Absinthe was first industrially produced at the end of the 18th century, and all through the 19th, it was incredibly popular. It was given a lift by a failed wine grape harvest in France, but by 1900 or so, everybody was drinking it. Vincent van Gogh, Oscar Wilde, Ernest Hemingway, Aleister Crowley… And because we know the movies would never lie to us, it doesn’t just get you drunk. The so-called “Green Fairy” makes you see things. I mean, we’ve all watched Moulin Rouge!… …What? Nicole Kidman? Ewan McGregor? Get on that! In the latter half of the 19th century, doctors began to characterize a condition they called absinthism, in which chronic consumption of absinthe was associated with hallucinations, convulsions, speech impairment, and even death. Much of this came from the work of a French physician named Valentin Magnan. And even by 19th century standards, his research methods weren’t amazing. He used wormwood essence rather than absinthe in his experiments, for one thing. He was even criticized in the pages of The Lancet, a prestigious medical journal that’s still around, in 1869. They pointed out that the symptoms he described couldn’t be distinguished from what we’d now call alcohol use disorder. Hold on to that thought. Nevertheless, this concept of absinthism gained traction, and got caught up in the larger temperance movement at the beginning of the 20th century. Absinthe was banned in the United States in 1912, as something of a dry run for Prohibition. Several European states outlawed absinthe starting in 1905, and France, although its people were consuming sixty liters of absinthe per person per year, joined the banned wagon in 1915. This year is usually seen as the official start of the absinthe ban. Having vanquished the Green Fairy and its evils for good, scientists turned to the question of what could have caused the terrible symptoms of absinthism. And for a while, they thought they had it. Wormwood contains a neurotoxic chemical called thujone. Thujone blocks the activity of receptors that bind the neurotransmitter GABAA. This leads to convulsions, although the dose required isn’t totally clear. Thujone is also in sage, incidentally, and is a good reason to be careful around essential oils containing sage, since there’s way more of it there than in absinthe. As we’re fond of saying around here, the dose makes the poison. One study in 1999 estimated that pre-ban absinthe could have contained up to 260 milligrams of thujone per liter, way above what we’d now consider safe. However… we’ll be revisiting this number later. For now, take it with a grain of salt. ...or cube of sugar? Anyway. So thujone seemed like a good candidate for causing the convulsions associated with absinthism. However, we searched the literature far and wide for evidence that it causes hallucinations. And if that evidence exists… we couldn’t find it. So in the name of being thorough, let’s explore a few other potential suspects… because that gives us the chance to talk about some more cool absinthe science, too. If you’ve never seen absinthe served in the traditional way, it’s great fun. You start with the absinthe in the glass with a sugar cube perched over it on a slotted spoon. You then pour water over the sugar cube and into the glass from a carafe, or better yet, a fancy fountain. If you’ve seen it lit on fire, that’s the bohemian tradition, which is different from the traditional tradition.
